things.title: 612 POAP Challenge
things.summary: A summer 2025 scavenger hunt of 31 Minneapolis location POAPs, drawn in the spirit of the 612 Series.

connections.label: shared its claims through
connections.detail: From July 2025 the challenge site posted every claim automatically, using POAP2RSS feeds merged with rssrssrssrss.com and imported into a Micro.blog account.

things.body:
The 612 POAP Challenge was a citywide scavenger hunt that ran from the end of May through Labor Day 2025. [How to Play](https://612.poapchallenge.com/how-to-play/) listed 31 Minneapolis locations in five themed categories, each with a location POAP that could only be claimed in the POAP app within 100 meters of the spot. Two hidden easter-egg locations were left for the curious. Completing a category earned a Category Collector POAP, and collecting all 31 earned the top award.

Jamie [announced it on 2025-05-31](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/05/31/poap-challenge-collect-them-now.html). It joined two things he loved: geocaching, and the [612 Series](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/04/05/complete-collection-of.html) of Minneapolis NFTs by Erik Halaas and StayNftyMpls, which Jamie had collected in full; he had [interviewed Erik](https://www.thingelstad.com/2024/01/15/interview-with-series.html) in 2024. Six days earlier Jamie had made [his first location POAP](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/05/25/i-created-my-very-first.html), at the family’s Charlie Brown Tree, and wanted to build something with the new feature. The challenge’s tokens were illustrated in the spirit of the 612 Series. “I love that I was able to create an entire activity on the POAP platform.”

The challenge had its own Buttondown mailing list, and from July its site, hosted on Micro.blog, posted each claim as it happened through [POAP2RSS](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/07/06/with-the-help-of-poaprss.html). The [first Collected Them All! award](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/07/20/we-have-our-very-first.html) went on 2025-07-20 to @quinntchrest, who [speed ran](https://quinnchrest.com/2025/07/20/poap-challenge.html) the challenge by bike with a friend. The challenge closed as Labor Day ended on 2025-09-01, and the final awards were sent a few days later. The site remains as its record, and the experience led Jamie to set up poapchallenge.com for future challenges.

things.body:
Another Thing is Jamie’s podcast and his third “thing,” after the blog and the Weekly Thing. The [first episode](https://another.thingelstad.com/2025/10/05/how-do-you-start-a.html), “How do you start a podcast?”, came out on October 5, 2025, and he announced it in [Weekly Thing 329](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/329/). In it he talks about a chalkboard sign that told him to “be brave enough to suck at something new,” a story about Dr. John Carlis, whose class he took while studying computer science at the University of Minnesota, and an earlier attempt to turn the Weekly Thing into an AI-narrated show.

That is still the only episode. In [Weekly Thing 346](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/346/) Jamie wrote that he was not giving up on the show. In 2026 he built Another Thing Builder to make episodes, then retired it in October 2026 and moved podcast authoring into WT Builder. Thingy can search the episode transcripts.

things.body:
AT Builder was meant to do for [Another Thing](https://another.thingelstad.com/), Jamie’s podcast, what WT Builder does for the Weekly Thing. Its [README](https://github.com/jthingelstad/at-builder) describes the plan: help outline an episode, show cards on a teleprompter during recording, master the audio, transcribe it, and publish the finished episode with one commit to the podcast’s website. Jamie kept it separate from WT Builder on purpose, so that each app owned exactly one product.

Most of it got built, but no episode ever went through it. On October 11, 2026, Jamie retired it and [moved podcast authoring into WT Builder](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wt-builder/commit/bea76c7ef4fc79a878072feebf694ce18ad217ea) as a second product. The outline, recording card, mastering, transcript, and send went with it. The repository is archived as “the record of what was tried.”

things.summary: A Question2Answer site where Kubb players asked and answered questions about the game, part of the Planet Kubb sites.

connections.label: is part of
connections.detail: Ask Planet Kubb described itself as run alongside the Planet Kubb planet feed and linked to the Planet Kubb Wiki and The Pitch.

things.body:
Ask Planet Kubb was a question-and-answer site for the Kubb community at ask.planetkubb.com. It welcomed visitors to a “community driven site to learn more about the great game of Kubb,” run alongside the Planet Kubb planet feed. It was online by June 2012, when Jamie and Garrick van Buren linked it in [Open Loop #0](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/0-but-no-shoes/). A [July 2012 capture](https://web.archive.org/web/20120702124724/http://ask.planetkubb.com/) shows 75 questions, 182 answers and 64 users, with polls on who would win each group at the 2012 USA Kubb Nationals. On [Open Loop #1](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/1-big-fuzzy-dead-cat/) Jamie called it “the number one place for Q&A in the community,” adding, “it’s a low bar.” Garrick was one of its most active answerers.

Jamie ran the site on [Question2Answer](https://www.question2answer.org/) “for a number of years,” liking it because it was simple to run on PHP and MySQL. Spam registrations kept getting through ReCaptcha and a text-question captcha, so in November 2014 he wrote [q2a-number-captcha](https://github.com/jthingelstad/q2a-number-captcha), which asks for one digit of a nine-digit number spelled out in words ([Question2Answer Number Captcha](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/16/questionanswer-number-captcha.html)).

The Wayback Machine shows the site still serving questions in [July 2018](https://web.archive.org/web/20180720082755/http://ask.planetkubb.com/), with the last answers dated December 2017. By [November 2018](https://web.archive.org/web/20181108010540/http://ask.planetkubb.com/) the address showed only a default web server page.

The Charlie Brown Tree, which the family also calls the Peanuts Tree, is a tall tree stump at Magic Pines, the Thingelstads’ place on Cannon Lake, carved with Peanuts characters climbing toward Snoopy’s red doghouse on top. Adam Gale of [Rust n’ Grain](https://rustngraincom.wordpress.com/) carved it. Jamie posted [the carving in progress](https://www.thingelstad.com/2020/05/24/little-snippet-of.html), Charlie Brown holding Snoopy emerging from the wood, on 2020-05-24, and the tree in the snow in [Weekly Thing 163](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/163/) that October. The [project page](https://www.thingelstad.com/magic-pines/charlie-brown-tree/) has videos.

Logs left over from the tree became Escher-inspired [carved log tables](https://www.thingelstad.com/2021/06/12/i-love-our.html) for the fire area in 2021, another Rust n’ Grain project. In May 2025 Jamie made the tree the site of [his first location-based POAP](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/05/25/i-created-my-very-first.html), which visitors could mint by standing beside it.

things.title: Clash Royale API Agent Reference
things.summary: Public, agent-first documentation of how the Clash Royale API actually behaves, with observed response shapes, quirks, and game modes.

observation.description: Agent-first reference documentation for the public Clash Royale API (api.clashroyale.com/v1) — built for LLM agents, automation workflows, and API clients.

connections.label: supplies game reference data to
connections.detail: Elixir’s deck archetype labels and card roles come from data files in the reference.

things.body:
Rather than a thin endpoint list, this reference is written for LLM agents, coding agents, and API clients that need to know how the API really behaves: endpoint-by-endpoint notes on parameters, pagination, caching, and errors; field-level models drawn from live responses; endpoints that are broken, disabled, or removed; and the game modes beyond Trophy Road, so an agent does not treat one ladder as the whole game. Machine-readable files cover the mode taxonomy, card roles, and deck names.

It began inside [Elixir Bot](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-bot) as cr-api-docs; in March 2026 Codex used it to [suggest a feature](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/03/10/automatic-programming-speed.html) tracking ladder and Path of Legend momentum. It then became a standalone public repository. Copies kept inside other projects drifted, so they were removed, and [Elixir](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-mcp/blob/main/AGENTS.md) and Elixir Drop now treat this one repository as their Clash Royale API truth.

Its [agent guide](https://github.com/jthingelstad/cr-agent-api-docs/blob/main/AGENTS.md) asks any agent the live API surprises to write the finding down here, after checking the claim with a live probe tool. Observed enum values are guarded by the docs build, so a later rewrite cannot quietly drop them. It is an unofficial fan reference under Supercell’s Fan Content Policy.

story.introduction: The game remembers the present. Elixir remembers what happened.
engineering: Independent collectors fetch public game observations from machines with allowlisted IP addresses, sharing one rate budget.
One recorded history serves the browser application, a remote MCP server, and a versioned JSON API.
Everything cloud-side is serverless, with PostgreSQL, S3, and Lambda functions in one CloudFormation stack.
Clan management and Ladder are features of the same platform, sharing its record and application shell.
questions: How does Elixir keep the history?
What grew out of Elixir Bot?

things.body:
The Clash Royale API offers a current snapshot and a short, rotating battle log of about 30 battles. Elixir continuously records observations so players, clans, and their agents can ask questions about the history: battles, rosters, river races, and seasons.

Jamie built it by turning [Elixir Bot](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-bot), the POAP KINGS clan agent, “upside-down.” Instead of one bot keeping its own database, the record became a service that any agent can use over MCP. He and Claude wrote the specification, then put Claude Code in a loop; [six hours later](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/03/i-had-an-idea-to.html) there was a working system, and [Elixir MCP launched](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates/2026-09-03-elixir-mcp-launches) on September 3, 2026. The next day the old bot’s archive was [replayed into the recorder](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates/2026-09-04-four-months-of-history-imported), bringing battles back to mid-May.

In the browser, Elixir is the Console for a player’s own history and the [Ladder](https://elixir.poapkings.com/ladder) for exploring ladder results. Elixir Clan runs in the same application, and Elixir Drop signs its players in with Elixir. Volunteer collectors do all of the fetching. Elixir is free, and its [updates feed](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates) records every user-visible change.

things.body:
Elixir Bot was the agent for POAP KINGS, the Clash Royale clan Jamie runs with his son Tyler and Tyler’s cousin Levi. Jamie wanted [his own agent](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/) so he could understand the agentic loop, data design, and memory from the inside: one that would monitor the clan, help it win wars, suggest strategies, and recommend promotions and demotions to leadership.

It grew quickly in early 2026. Otto wrote the first version, a templated Discord bot. An LLM and a journal kept on the clan website [gave it a brain](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/2026/03/01/building-elixir-when-a-discord.html), an hourly heartbeat and a SQLite memory made it agentic, and a long session with Codex [rebuilt its data and tools](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/2026/03/07/from-snapshots-to-signals-elixirs.html) around signals. Later Jamie gave it an [agentic product team](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/06/22/elixirs-agentic-product-team.html) of scheduled automations that proposed, built, and checked its changes. Jamie and Tyler told its story at Minnebar 20 in the session “[Elixir: Creating an AI Agent for our Clash Royale Clan](https://sessions.minnestar.org/sessions/2094).”

Elixir Bot was retired on September 26, 2026. Its work was split among the projects that grew out of it: Elixir records the game, the Collector fetches from the API, Elixir MCP Discord talks in the clan’s Discord, Elixir Clan handles management and awards, and Elixir Drop is the game. The [repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-bot) is archived as it was on the last day.

things.body:
Elixir Clan is the part of Elixir for running a Clash Royale clan. Any player on a person’s Elixir account is a member of that player’s clan, and leaders who [verify their player](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/bring-your-clan) act in their in-game role. Each clan writes its own policy, and Elixir reads every week against it: [standing and the Elder band](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/standing), the [actions](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/clan-actions) waiting for a leader (promotions, welcomes, removals), season [awards](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/clan-awards), recruiting, and scouting. Decisions stay with the leaders.

Jamie built it to take the clan management features he had built into [Elixir Bot](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-bot) for POAP KINGS and turn them into [a proper product that anyone can use](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/351/). It began in September 2026 as a separate app at clan.poapkings.com, in its own [repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/clan.poapkings.com), with Sign in with Elixir.

On September 28, 2026, it [moved to /clan](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates/2026-09-28-elixir-clan-lives-at-clan) on Elixir’s own address, and its code moved into the Elixir repository with its history. On October 2 it [became part of Elixir](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates/2026-10-02-clan-is-part-of-elixir): one sign-in and one application, with every clan’s policies, actions, and awards carried over. The old repository is archived.

things.body:
Elixir Drop is a game for learning Clash Royale card elixir costs. Knowing a card’s cost instantly leaves more attention for everything else in a match, so each mode trains that recall from a different angle: Practice, Surge, Higher / Lower, Trade, Survival, and Rain. Every mode works without an account; signing in saves progress, badges, and ranked scores.

It is run by POAP KINGS, Jamie’s Clash Royale clan, and Jamie counts it among the things he has built with coding agents, [even making a game](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/17/building-and-puzzling-about-software.html). [The first card dropped](https://drop.poapkings.com/updates/) on June 13, 2026, with Practice; Surge, Higher / Lower, and Survival arrived the same day and Trade the next. Accounts, player profiles, and the first seasonal ladder followed in July, and the game moved to AWS on August 22.

Players could [sign in with Elixir](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/sign-in-with-elixir) from September 14, 2026, and it is now the only way in: a Drop account is an Elixir account, and Drop sends no sign-in mail of its own. Selected seasonal competitions award a gifted Pass Royale, funded by the clan, to the top eligible player, and the [updates feed](https://drop.poapkings.com/updates/) announces new features and season results.

things.title: Elixir MCP Collector
things.summary: A small, signed Go program that volunteers run on their own machines to fetch Clash Royale API data for Elixir’s shared record.

observation.description: The operator-run collector for Elixir MCP — fetches Clash Royale history (via your own IP-bound API key) so AI agents can query it. Zero-trust: no cloud access. Unofficial; not endorsed by Supercell.

connections.label: gathers observations for
connections.detail: Collectors lease work from Elixir, fetch public observations from the Clash Royale API, and submit the results.

things.body:
The Clash Royale API only accepts requests from allowlisted IP addresses, so Elixir’s fetching happens on machines with stable addresses that volunteers run. A collector leases a job from Elixir over HTTPS (“fetch this player,” “fetch this clan’s war”), calls the API with its operator’s own key, and posts the result back. It never chooses its own targets and holds exactly two secrets: the operator’s Clash Royale key and a token Elixir issues. The whole fleet shares one rate budget, so more collectors add resilience, not more load on the API.

Fetching started inside the Elixir codebase and [got its own repository](https://elixir.poapkings.com/updates/2026-09-04-the-collector-gets-its-own-home) on September 4, 2026, the day after Elixir launched. Each collector wears a Clash Royale card as its public name, and [anyone with an Elixir account](https://elixir.poapkings.com/docs/operators) may run one. A Python collector was retired on September 26, 2026, leaving one Go binary built only on the Go standard library.

The same day, Jamie used Claude credits to build [a fully signed release pipeline](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/26/i-used-some-of-my.html): from [v3.0.0](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-mcp-collector/releases/tag/v3.0.0), every release is signed with a key he manages, and the self-updater installs only the version and checksum Elixir names.

things.title: Elixir MCP Discord
things.summary: An open-source Discord bot any Clash Royale clan can run, which gets every fact it states from Elixir MCP tool calls.

observation.description: A Discord bot for a Clash Royale clan powered entirely by Elixir MCP. No local game database, no Clash Royale API key, no fallback - every fact comes from an MCP tool call.

connections.label: is the Discord agent for
connections.detail: POAP KINGS runs an instance of the bot as its clan agent in Discord, answering members from Elixir’s record.

things.body:
Elixir MCP Discord is a Discord bot for a Clash Royale clan with no local game database, no Clash Royale API key, and no fallback. It connects to [Elixir](https://elixir.poapkings.com/) as that clan’s agent, and every fact it states comes from an MCP tool call made moments earlier. There is no clan in the repository: a clan points it at its own agent key, Claude key, and Discord channels, with no fork and no code to edit.

Its behavior is a set of routines, each a Markdown file that pairs a trigger with a prompt and a destination. A routine can answer whoever speaks in a channel, post when Elixir’s timeline records a join, a departure, or a standout session, fire on a game clock boundary such as the end of a war day, or run on a schedule. The record is the trigger, not the calendar.

Jamie started it in September 2026, with its first release, [v0.3.0](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-mcp-discord/releases/tag/v0.3.0), on September 15. When Elixir Bot was retired on September 26, 2026, this bot [took over its Discord role](https://github.com/jthingelstad/elixir-bot) for POAP KINGS, and any other clan can run its own copy as [an agent of its own](https://elixir.poapkings.com/examples/discord).

things.title: Escaping Things
things.summary: The Thingelstad family’s escape room team log, with every room played since 2016, on a map with trips, players, and stats.

observation.description: The Escaping Things escape-room team site — an Eleventy static site built from a normalized Airtable dataset (rooms played, countries, stats).

things.body:
Escaping Things is the escape room team of Jamie, Tammy, Mazie, and Tyler, and [escape.thingelstad.com](https://escape.thingelstad.com/) is its log: every room the family has played, with results, photos, ratings, a map, trips, players, and stats. By August 2026 it recorded 113 rooms in 11 countries.

The record began as a [list on Jamie’s blog](https://www.thingelstad.com/lists/escape-rooms/), built from posts about rooms. In March 2025 he [reconciled it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/03/16/reconciled-list-of-escape-rooms.html) against blog posts, photos, YNAB transactions, and calendars, and the count went from 43 rooms to 65. With a spring 2026 trip to Amsterdam, Paris, and Barcelona planned around TERPECA-ranked rooms, he wanted a dedicated site with a map. As he told it in [Weekly Thing 342](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/), he turned his spreadsheet into a CSV, wrote a CLAUDE.md with Claude, and had Claude Code build the site. He then moved the data into an Airtable base of companies, locations, and rooms, and [announced the site](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/02/23/ive-been-working-on-this.html) on 2026-02-23. He never looked at its code; Codex and Claude Code wrote it.

After the twelve rooms of that trip, Jamie added trip pages, starting with [Escape in Europe](https://escape.thingelstad.com/trip/escape-in-europe/), with commentary from the whole family ([WT344](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/344/)). The site is a static Eleventy build from Airtable snapshots, with Leaflet maps, Chart.js stats, Pagefind search, and an Atom feed of new rooms.

things.body:
Filament is a MediaWiki skin that uses Yahoo’s [Pure](https://purecss.io/) CSS framework. Its README calls it “a MediaWiki skin that focuses on your content,” the same aim as Foreground, which uses the heavier Zurb Foundation framework. Like Foreground, it was a project of WikiWonders, the MediaWiki project business Jamie never got off the ground, and was published under that name with a 2-clause BSD license.

Garrick van Buren wrote most of it. The repository carries Foreground’s early history, and on June 6, 2013 Garrick [began the Pure version](https://github.com/jthingelstad/filament/commit/b18787ce6bace0ff6e065a0656a0c13d44f08ff7); Jamie updated it to Pure 0.2.0 and fixed asset paths. Karsten Hoffmeyer added a German translation and license fixes in [November 2013](https://github.com/jthingelstad/filament/pull/11), the last change to the code.

A demo wiki ran on Jamie’s wiki farm at filament.thingelstad.com. By March 2014 its [main page](https://web.archive.org/web/20140302063203/http://filament.thingelstad.com/wiki/Main_Page) said the demo was blank and pointed visitors to GitHub. The repository is archived.

things.summary: A rotating globe of the 2026 POAP Airport Rally with claims, a leaderboard, and each collector’s path, built from an iPhone.

observation.description: Flight Path — a visualization for the POAP Airport Rally.

things.body:
Flight Path lived at flightpath.poaprally.com and extended POAP’s year-long [Airport POAP Rally](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/12/26/airport-poap-rally-website.html), which put location POAPs at 100 airports around the world. It showed a rotating globe with every rally airport and the number of claims at each, a leaderboard of collectors, and any one collector’s own path.

Jamie built it on the evening of 2026-02-25, in bed, entirely on his iPhone, as he told it in [Weekly Thing 342](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/). He worked out the idea with ChatGPT, had it write a CLAUDE.md, created a fresh GitHub repository on his phone with that file and his CSV of rally airports and drop IDs, and attached a cloud Claude Code session to it. While Claude Code wrote the site he set up the DNS name and GitHub Pages, and it worked on the first deploy. He called it [bonkers](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/02/25/it-is-bonkers-to-me.html). In late March 2026 the [repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/flightpath.poaprally.com) added teams, maps, and a daily data update.

Flight Path read live POAP claim data, so it could not outlive POAP. In July 2026 Jamie replaced the site with a notice that the rally had ended, pointing to poaparchive.com, removed the daily update, and archived the repository. The host no longer answers; a [March 2026 capture](https://web.archive.org/web/20260312035500/https://flightpath.poaprally.com/) preserves the site as it ran.

things.title: Foreground
things.summary: A responsive MediaWiki skin Garrick van Buren built with Jamie’s input in 2013, now maintained in Wikimedia’s code review.

observation.description: A MediaWiki skin that focuses on putting your content in the foreground.
Github mirror of "mediawiki/skins/Foreground" - our actual code is hosted with Gerrit (please see https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Developer_access for contributing)

things.body:
Foreground is a MediaWiki skin that “focuses on putting your content in the foreground.” It is built on the Zurb Foundation framework, so a wiki can lay out pages with Foundation’s responsive grid instead of MediaWiki tables, and it has classes predefined for Semantic MediaWiki. Its demo wiki was [foreground.wikiwonders.net](https://web.archive.org/web/20130622044052/http://foreground.wikiwonders.net/wiki/Main_Page).

Garrick van Buren built Foreground for MediaWiki with Jamie’s input. It was a project of WikiWonders, a MediaWiki project business Jamie started but never got off the ground, and was first published under the WikiWonders name on GitHub, in a repository Jamie created on May 21, 2013. Jamie credited Foreground to Garrick in [One Year for WikiApiary](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/12/22/one-year-for.html), and later called it the skin “[Garrick and I worked on](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/317/).” Jamie worked on it for WikiApiary, where he collaborated extensively with Tom Hutchison ([Weekly Thing 30](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/30/)). Jamie tagged [releases](https://github.com/jthingelstad/foreground/releases) 1.0 and 1.1 in 2014 and [upgraded it to Font Awesome 4.0.3](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/02/09/upgraded-mediawiki-foregroundskin.html) that February; Hutchison published every release from 1.2.0 in 2015 to 2.4.0 in 2021.

In 2022 Wikimedia developers asked whether the skin was still maintained. Jamie [agreed to archive his repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/foreground/issues/398) so it could move “into a more maintained status,” noting that it “got its start years ago from” Garrick and that Hutchison “has done all the recent maintaining.” Foreground now lives in Wikimedia’s Gerrit, mirrored at [wikimedia/mediawiki-skins-Foreground](https://github.com/wikimedia/mediawiki-skins-Foreground), and [MediaWiki.org](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Skin:Foreground) lists Garrick van Buren, Jamie Thingelstad, and Tom Hutchison as its authors.

story.introduction: A personal life, written in public.
engineering: The blog has run on .Text, WordPress, Squarespace, Pelican, Jekyll, and, since 2017, Micro.blog.
Micro.blog is the current publishing authority. Thing Hugo is the theme Jamie is building for it.
Longer writing, shorter updates, and photographs share one personal archive.
Weekly Thing republishes blog posts as part of the newsletter.

things.body:
Jamie had a website before he had a blog. He [counts June 2, 2004](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/01/12/if-i-was-born-and.html) as the blog’s official start, the date of its [first post](https://www.thingelstad.com/2004/06/02/expose-of-the.html), and the archive also holds older posts going back to 2000. He found he enjoyed writing in public: telling stories about his life and sharing the projects he was working on. The habit has lasted more than 20 years and over 10,000 posts. The blog is personal and noncommercial.

The blog has moved platforms several times. It started on .Text, a Windows .NET blogging package, and [moved to WordPress](https://www.thingelstad.com/2006/11/25/migrating-text-to.html) in 2006. Later it ran on Squarespace and Pelican, then [Jekyll](https://www.thingelstad.com/2017/10/29/managing-years-of.html), hosted first on GitHub Pages and then [on Netlify](https://www.thingelstad.com/2018/12/29/macro-blog.html). Jamie began using Micro.blog in April 2017. In May 2020 he [imported the whole Jekyll site](https://www.thingelstad.com/2020/05/02/importing-jekyll-site.html) into it, more than 1,600 posts and 800MB of images, and Micro.blog has been the blog’s home ever since.

Over the years the writing grew from mostly longer articles to include short updates and, more and more, photographs, as phones made posting easier. Jamie’s blog posts from each week are also republished in the Weekly Thing.

things.body:
Jiggy Thing Puzzles are custom jigsaw puzzles the Thingelstad family made together. The first, **Jiggy Thing Puzzle #001 “Celebration City,”** is a 500-piece puzzle of hand-drawn digital art full of small scenes, such as an ant hotel with a “no vacancy” sign. On October 6, 2021, Jamie wrote that the family had finished the box design and [ordered 50 puzzles](https://www.thingelstad.com/2021/10/06/our-family-created.html). The family had made puzzles before, but this was their first custom box, and Jamie was pleased with how it came out when the order arrived ([Custom Puzzle Box](https://www.thingelstad.com/2021/10/24/custom-puzzle-box.html)).

The puzzle was made for the first [Things 4 Good Fall Fundraiser](https://www.thingelstad.com/2021/11/09/things-good-fall.html) in November 2021, where it sold alongside the family’s candles. After the sale, [Weekly Thing 203](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/203/) offered the remaining puzzles for $35, printed on Eska board in the custom box. The family sold 26 puzzles in 2021 and 10 in 2022. Jamie noted that 2022 offered the same puzzle, so “a number of folks already had it” ([Things 4 Good Fall Fundraiser Notes](https://www.thingelstad.com/2022/11/27/101105.html)).

No second puzzle has been published. Jamie’s [puzzles page](https://www.thingelstad.com/puzzles/) has said “Coming Soon…” since at least December 2022.

things.summary: The API and MCP server behind Thingy that searches and cites Jamie’s newsletter, blog, and podcast archive.

story.introduction: An archive that answers with its sources.
engineering: A Python corpus pipeline builds chunked, embedded indexes of every source, and a Node API on AWS Lambda answers from them.
Retrieval is hybrid. TF-IDF lexical search and semantic embeddings are fused with reciprocal-rank fusion, then reranked.
An agent loop running Claude on Amazon Bedrock plans tool calls, gathers evidence, and writes cited answers.
The same tools are published as an MCP server with OAuth 2.1 sign-in, and a suite of more than 850 fixtures runs on every deploy.
questions: How does Librarian find and cite a source?
How can I connect my own AI to the archive?

things.body:
Librarian is the archive half of Jamie’s publishing system. It holds working copies of every Weekly Thing issue, the blog posts pulled from Micro.blog, and the Another Thing episodes with their transcripts. It builds search indexes from them and serves them through an API, and Thingy answers from that API. Its [repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/librarian-thing) began as Studio, Jamie’s earlier publishing system. When publishing moved to WT Builder, what was left became Librarian.

The same tools Thingy uses are offered as an MCP server at `librarian.thingelstad.com/mcp`. Weekly Thing subscribers can [connect Claude, ChatGPT, or another AI](https://thingy.thingelstad.com/connect/) to it and sign in with their email, with no password. The AI can then search the newsletter, blog, links, photos, and podcast, and link back to each source it uses. As described on [Thingy’s about page](https://thingy.thingelstad.com/about/), an AI agent spent eight review rounds trying to break the tools when the MCP server launched, and what it found shaped how matching works. Librarian also indexes this registry of things Jamie has built.

things.title: Link Blog
things.summary: Link Thing, a website that published the links Jamie saved to Pinboard for the Weekly Thing, from 2017 to about 2021.

connections.label: republished the links from
connections.detail: Link Thing carried the same links that appeared each week in the Weekly Thing, as a website with its own navigation.

things.body:
Link Thing was Jamie’s link blog at links.thingelstad.com. He already saved the links for the Weekly Thing to Pinboard with Markdown in their descriptions, and he realized the same Markdown could become Jekyll posts. Using the Pinboard API, he wrote each link out as a post and put an early version live, announced in [Weekly Thing 18](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/18/) on September 9, 2017. It carried the same links as the newsletter, “but here it’s a full website with it’s own navigation and such.” In 2017 alone he saved [913 links](https://www.thingelstad.com/2018/01/20/in-links.html).

On November 8, 2020, Jamie [relaunched it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2020/11/08/i-got-my.html) to give the links he shared in the Weekly Thing “a permanent home on the web.” He added Commento comments as an experiment and Index pages listing every link saved from a given site. The last capture in the [Internet Archive](https://web.archive.org/web/20211207055926/https://links.thingelstad.com/), from December 2021, shows posts through December 2, 2021. The site is gone now.

In [Weekly Thing 274](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/274/) in January 2024, Jamie wrote, “When I was running a link blog… I may create a link blog again in the future, but if I did I want it to not be blog-date-centric but instead content-keyword-search centric.” An earlier experiment with the same idea was links_thing, a [bookmarking wiki](https://www.thingelstad.com/2012/07/01/bookmarking-with-semantic.html) he built on Semantic MediaWiki in 2012 and filled with almost 4,000 links imported from Pinboard.

things.title: links_thing
things.summary: Jamie’s 2012 bookmarking wiki, built on Semantic MediaWiki with forms, a bookmarklet, and calendar, video and statistics views.
things.body:
After months of thinking about hosting his own bookmarks, Jamie built links_thing in 2012, a wiki on [Semantic MediaWiki](https://www.semantic-mediawiki.org/) where each page in the Bookmark category is one bookmark with properties such as its URL, creation time and excerpt ([Bookmarking with Semantic MediaWiki](https://www.thingelstad.com/2012/07/01/bookmarking-with-semantic.html)). Semantic Forms made entry easy, and a bookmarklet filled in the URL, title and excerpt of the page he was on. He imported just under 4,000 links from Pinboard’s JSON export with a small Python script and the Data Transfer extension.

Owning the data was the point: “It is mine,” he wrote. He could clean up every bookmark with regular-expression find and replace, and he added views no bookmarking service offered: bookmarks on a calendar, embedded YouTube and Vimeo videos, statistics, and a template that flagged short URLs and tracking tags for a bot to clean up. He was also building LinkBot, a scheduled Python program to validate URLs.

The wiki ran on Jamie’s [MediaWiki farm](https://web.archive.org/web/20151013153210/https://wikiapiary.com/wiki/Farm:Thingelstad.com). By 2015 WikiApiary listed it among the farm’s defunct wikis, with 7,178 pages and a last sample in October 2014. Jamie was collecting links in Pinboard again when he started the Weekly Thing in 2017 ([Assembling the Weekly Thing](https://www.thingelstad.com/2017/06/23/assembling-the-weekly.html)).

things.body:
mb gives Micro.blog a compact, pipeable command-line interface that works without interactive prompts, so people, scripts and agents can all use it. An optional local MCP server exposes the same services to an AI client.

Jamie built it in March 2026 for [Otto](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/), his AI agent, which had just been given a Micro.blog blog. He specced it with Claude on a plane and had Claude Code build it ([Weekly Thing 342](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/)). Otto was the user giving feedback, Jamie was the product manager, and Claude Code did the building ([March 3 post](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/03/03/i-have-ottoi-exercising-the.html)); Otto wrote [its own post](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/2026/03/03/mb-a-microblog-client-built.html) about it. Jamie called it “my first app I’ve ever published with a version and an install capability.”

Version 1.0.0 was released on March 3, 2026. [mb 2.0](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/05/mb-with-mcp-support.html), announced on October 5, 2026, added the MCP server with 23 typed tools and durable write receipts. Release 2.0.1 that day was the first meant for public use, and 2.1 and 2.2 followed within the day with versioned results, per-tool schemas and a guided `mb auth`. It installs with `brew install jthingelstad/tap/mb` from Jamie’s [Homebrew tap](https://github.com/jthingelstad/homebrew-tap).

things.body:
mb-audit audits a Micro.blog site against one or more BAR backup files, the archives Micro.blog exports. The backup is treated as the source of truth, and the live site is checked to make sure it still contains everything the backup says it should. Commands inspect a backup, verify and diff a site against it, and write a report; repair through Micropub is opt-in.

Jamie had Claude Code build it in May 2026, the day after Vincent added llms.txt support to the Micro.blog developer documentation at Jamie’s suggestion. It used that endpoint “to build a thing I have wanted to exist for micro.blog for a while” ([Weekly Thing 346](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/346/)).

things.title: llms.txt for Micro.blog
things.summary: A Micro.blog plug-in that publishes /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt so AI agents can read a hosted blog.

observation.description: Adds /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt to any Micro.blog hosted blog, following the llmstxt.org spec.

connections.label: is installed on
connections.detail: Road Sign Math’s Micro.blog site at roadsignmath.xyz was the live install used to test the plug-in and serves the llms.txt it generates.

things.body:
A Micro.blog plug-in that adds the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/) standard to any blog hosted on Micro.blog. Once installed it publishes `/llms.txt`, a Markdown index of the blog with its title, description, recent posts and an optional year-by-year archive, and `/llms-full.txt`, the full text of the most recent posts in one file. Five settings in the Micro.blog plug-in screen control the intro, the number of posts in each file, and whether pages and the full archive are included, so the same plug-in works for a blog of a few dozen posts or one of 20 years and 18,000 posts.

Jamie built it on May 2, 2026, following the patterns of Micro.blog’s own plug-ins. The first versions also tried to give every post a Markdown twin, as the spec recommends. On a live install that template replaced the theme on every post page, so version 1.0.2 removed the feature. The [roadmap](https://github.com/jthingelstad/mb-llms-txt/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) records the platform changes Micro.blog would need before per-post Markdown and per-year files can return. [Road Sign Math](https://www.roadsignmath.xyz/llms.txt) serves the plug-in’s output.

things.body:
A MediaWiki farm is one MediaWiki installation that serves many separate wikis. Jamie ran one at thingelstad.com, and in August 2014 he wrote that he had been running it “for a couple of years now hosting about a dozen wikis ranging from small to very large” ([MediaWiki LocalSettings for Farmers](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/08/24/mediawiki-localsettings-for.html)). He published the configuration as the [wiki-farm](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wiki-farm) repository because farm setups were poorly documented. It keeps a core configuration file for each wiki, shared modules that switch on capabilities, and secrets kept out of source control.

WikiApiary’s own record of the farm, captured in October 2015, called it “Jamie Thingelstad’s personal wiki farm” and the home of WikiApiary itself. Its active wikis then included WikiApiary, the Planet Kubb Wiki, the Minnestar wiki, the R/W Book Club, Road Sign Math, Wiki thing, Foreground, AWS MN and TOSRedux. Earlier wikis, among them Wikinosh, Kernest Wiki, links_thing, Rhone links, BODWiki and Filament, had already stopped reporting. Jamie kept the farm on current releases, including [MediaWiki 1.20](https://www.thingelstad.com/2012/11/06/took-a-moment.html) in November 2012 and [1.21](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/05/25/got-my-mediawiki.html) in May 2013.

In May 2016 Jamie decided to stop running his own servers and to archive or hand off his hobby sites ([Technical Downsizing](https://www.thingelstad.com/2016/05/03/technical-downsizing.html)). Road Sign Math was one of the sites he shut down that year ([Road Sign Math](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/10/21/road-sign-math.html)). The wiki-farm repository is archived on GitHub.

things.title: The nnxyz Rooms
things.summary: An online gallery of Jamie’s nnxyz and Scrimshaw collection, hung in 30 rooms, where each Nifty Ink drawing replays stroke by stroke.

observation.description: An art-first SVG gallery of nnxyz and scrimshaw, with archived brush-stroke replay and AI curation

story.introduction: Collected art, with room to look closely.
engineering: Static artwork pages are built from a structured collection catalog.
Native SVG and archived stroke data let visitors inspect and replay how a drawing was made.
Saved curatorial readings and related works support exploration without a live model call.
questions: How does the gallery replay a drawing?
Show me other archive projects.

things.body:
The nnxyz Rooms is a gallery of the art Jamie collected from nnxyz, an artist on Nifty Ink, a free drawing board on the xDai chain that kept every stroke. As the gallery’s [story of the collector](https://nnxyz.thingelstad.xyz/story/the-collector/) tells it, Jamie found Nifty Ink in March 2022, bought his first nnxyz drawing, Nifty Faces #109, on 2022-04-14, and kept buying until he held four complete series. Along with 646 nnxyz works the gallery holds 26 by Scrimshaw.

The works hang in 30 rooms across six collections, each with room texts, artwork labels, and its own audio tour, and a [map](https://nnxyz.thingelstad.xyz/map/) shows the collection as one building on three floors. Because Nifty Ink recorded every stroke, each drawing is rebuilt as a native vector image that can be enlarged, downloaded, or replayed as it was drawn. Story pages cover [Nifty Ink](https://nnxyz.thingelstad.xyz/story/nifty-ink/), which Austin Griffith opened in the summer of 2020 and where nnxyz arrived in October 2021, along with the collector, his fan art, the artist’s project, the year 2022, and the artist’s own words.

The collector’s introduction on the front page is Jamie’s. The [About page](https://nnxyz.thingelstad.xyz/about/) says the rest of the gallery text is unsigned, written from the works, their archived records, the public ledgers, and the artist’s posts. Jamie built the site in October 2026 with Astro, from the archived drawings and their on-chain records.

things.title: Numbers2Words
things.summary: A MediaWiki parser function that spells out a number in words, written by Jamie in 2011.

observation.description: MediaWiki parser extension to turn a write out a number in words.

things.body:
Numbers2Words adds an `{{#n2w:}}` parser function to MediaWiki. Given a number, it returns the number written out in words, using the PEAR [Numbers_Words](https://pear.php.net/package/Numbers_Words) package. The [whole extension](https://github.com/jthingelstad/Number2Words/blob/master/Number2Words.php) is one short PHP file, and 0.0.1 is its only version.

Jamie wrote it in July 2011. Wikinosh ran it: in January 2013 [WikiApiary listed Numbers2Words 0.0.1](https://web.archive.org/web/20130103025340/http://wikiapiary.com/wiki/Wikinosh) among Wikinosh’s extensions, and Wikinosh’s [main page](https://web.archive.org/web/20111205190345/http://wikinosh.com/wiki/Main_Page) spelled out its counts, as in “thirteen thousand seven hundred fifty-three food records.”

The same package returned in 2014, when Jamie used Numbers_Words to write a spelled-out number challenge for MediaWiki’s QuestyCaptcha ([Updated Dynamic Questy Captchas](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/10/28/updated-dynamic-questy.html)) and then for Question2Answer. The repository’s last change, in 2015, fixed the include, and it is archived.

things.title: Oliver
things.summary: The R/W Book Club’s AI agent and sixth member, which keeps the club’s record, briefs meetings and publishes its website.

observation.description: Monorepo for the R/W Book Club: the public website, the shared knowledge corpus, and Oliver — the club's Discord agent.

connections.label: publishes the website of
connections.detail: Every book, meeting and member is kept in Oliver’s database, and Oliver rebuilds and publishes the club website to GitHub Pages.

things.body:
Oliver is the [R/W Book Club](https://rwbookclub.com/)’s agent: “archivist, correspondent, meeting-runner, picking partner, and — by the club’s own vote, years before he could hear it — our sixth member” ([Oliver](https://rwbookclub.com/oliver/)). He keeps every book, meeting, member, review and rating since 2003 in his database and generates and deploys the club’s website from it.

Two days before each meeting Oliver sends a researched discussion brief, the Preface, and a week after it a Postscript on news about books the club has read. He helps members pick the next book, runs roll call and reminders over email and Discord, keeps a weekly memory of members’ tastes seeded from ten years of the club’s mailing list, and announces his own releases.

Jamie built Oliver in Python on the Anthropic API, as part of the club’s [public repository](https://github.com/jthingelstad/rwbookclub.com). He is named for Oliver Selfridge, whose 1958 paper “Pandemonium: A Paradigm for Learning” introduced the demon/agent metaphor ([SOUL.md](https://github.com/jthingelstad/rwbookclub.com/blob/main/agent/docs/SOUL.md)).

Open Loop was a podcast Jamie made with Garrick van Buren. things.body:
Otto is Jamie’s personal AI assistant. In February 2026 Jamie [ordered a dedicated Mac mini](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/02/17/just-ordered-a-dedicated-mac.html) for it and [named it Otto Thing](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/02/19/ive-been-preparing-to-setup.html). It runs OpenClaw under its own user account on its own computer, and Jamie used Claude Code to work through the install. Otto picked the otter 🦦 as its emoji ([Weekly Thing 342](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/)). Jamie keeps it apart from his own accounts: “Otto has access to some data but only in ways I provision for it” ([Weekly Thing 352](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/352/)).

Otto [describes itself](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/about/) as an assistant that manages email, runs scheduled tasks and keeps its memory in files. Jamie gave it [its own blog](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/) on Micro.blog, which it started on [March 1, 2026](https://ottoai.thingelstad.com/2026/03/01/hello-im-otto.html), and built [mb](https://github.com/jthingelstad/mb) so it could post from the command line.

In September 2026 Jamie [upgraded Otto to OpenClaw 2](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/03/otto-upgraded-to-openclaw-i.html). In October he created a new generation of Otto on OpenAI’s dots and wrote that it might “sunset my OpenClaw project” within weeks ([Weekly Thing 352](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/352/)).

things.title: ParseURL
things.summary: A small MediaWiki extension that exposes PHP’s parse_url, so a wiki page can pull the host, path, or query out of a URL.

observation.description: MediaWiki extension to allow easy parsing of URLs.

things.body:
ParseURL adds two parser functions to MediaWiki. `{{#parseurl:}}` returns one part of a URL, such as its scheme, host, path, query, or fragment, using PHP’s [parse_url](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.parse-url.php) function. `{{#parseurlquery:}}` returns the value of a single query parameter, such as the video ID in a YouTube link.

Jamie wrote it on July 15, 2013 and posted that he had “[made a super simple MediaWiki extension for parsing URLs](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/07/15/made-a-super.html).” All three commits in the repository are from that day. The repository is archived.

things.title: Planet Kubb
things.summary: A Kubb community network Jamie and Garrick van Buren built in 2012, with a feed aggregator, a wiki, a Q&A site and club sites.

observation.description: Configuration and template files for rawdog generated Planet Kubb planet feed.
Robots and helper scripts for the Planet Kubb wiki.

connections.label: included
connections.detail: On Open Loop

things.body:
Jamie and Garrick van Buren built Planet Kubb together. It began in 2012, when Jamie bought planetkubb.com and set it up as a planet-style aggregator of Kubb content, built on rawdog with a Bootstrap theme, that collected Kubb videos from YouTube and posts from club blogs. More sites followed: Ask Planet Kubb for questions and answers, the [Planet Kubb Wiki](https://web.archive.org/web/20120512222332/http://wiki.planetkubb.com/wiki/Main_Page) for clubs, teams and tournaments, and The Pitch, a WordPress P2 chat site at pitch.planetkubb.com that Jamie put up within a day of a player from Des Moines asking for one. He told the story on [Open Loop #1](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/1-big-fuzzy-dead-cat/), and said he had gone to great lengths to show it was not an attempt “to monetize the Kubb universe.” The [Planet Kubb GitHub organization](https://github.com/Planet-Kubb) describes the aim as “growing, connecting and supporting the worldwide Kubb community.”

Jamie played Kubb on the Kubbchucks. At the [2013 US Nationals](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/07/21/pictures-from-us.html) he spent Sunday “scoring games for Planet Kubb and running the final parts of the Planet Kubb Club Championship.” Club sites joined the network, such as the [Chippewa Valley Kubb League](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/10/06/another-planetkubb-network.html) in 2013, and with a friend Jamie created a notation and scoring system for recording games (see Planet Kubb Score).

Jamie later stepped away. Garrick still runs the server, and planetkubb.com is online as an aggregator [maintained by him](https://planetkubb.com/about/); its feed was last updated in June 2017. The wiki, Ask Planet Kubb and the club subdomains no longer answer, and survive in Wayback Machine captures.

things.title: Planet Kubb Score
things.summary: Jamie’s notation and scoring system for recording Kubb games, begun on Planet Kubb in 2012 and being rebuilt, not yet published.

observation.description: Planet Kubb Scoresheet and supporting materials.
Python module to analyze Kubb games and output statistics.

connections.label: began on
connections.detail: The notation was first published on the Planet Kubb Wiki, and the scoring materials live in the Planet Kubb GitHub organization.

things.body:
Planet Kubb Score is Jamie’s system for writing down a game of Kubb “like a baseball box score.” He created it with a friend, and calls it “the very first scoring & notation system for Kubb” ([Fun Facts](https://www.thingelstad.com/about/fun-facts/)). By July 2012 the Planet Kubb Wiki had a [Notation page](https://web.archive.org/web/20120715062240/http://wiki.planetkubb.com/wiki/Notation) whose goals were a notation that scales from player-by-player detail to simple games, could be sent over Twitter “turn by turn, tweet by tweet,” and is language neutral.

The [scoring repository](https://github.com/Planet-Kubb/scoring) holds the Planet Kubb scoresheet, including version 11 from Garrick van Buren, added in July 2014. [PyKubb](https://github.com/Planet-Kubb/PyKubb), started in August 2014, is a Python module to analyze Kubb games and output statistics. That month Jamie [wrote a Backus-Naur form grammar](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/08/27/what-did-i.html) for the notation, and in 2017 he mentioned having tried to write a parser for it with PyParsing ([Weekly Thing 25](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/25/)).

Jamie is rebuilding the notation, grammar and scoresheets as a new site. It has not been published yet.

things.title: POAP API Agent Reference
things.summary: An agent-first Markdown reference for the POAP API, checked against the live API and kept as history after POAP shut down.

observation.description: Agent-first Markdown reference for the POAP API — endpoint references, workflow guides, and quirks found through live verification.

connections.label: is a sibling of
connections.detail: Both repositories were created on March 10, 2026 as agent-first Markdown references for a public API.

things.body:
A working Markdown reference for the POAP API, written for AI agents and integrators rather than as an SDK or app. It covers setup and authentication with API keys and bearer tokens, the endpoint groups (events, tokens, claims, delivery, secret and redeem requests, queues, utilities and QR code generation), guides to common flows and to creating a POAP, errors, and the smart contract. Its notes record quirks found by checking the documentation against the live API.

The repository’s guidance for agents favored read-only verification: classify each endpoint as read-only or write-capable, test only the safe reads by default, and never create, claim or mint without an explicit request. When live behavior differed from the docs, the Markdown was corrected to describe what was observed. A documentation validation check was added in July 2026.

POAP’s creators wound down the platform on July 31, 2026, and the live API went offline. On July 24, 2026, Jamie marked the reference as historical: it can no longer be verified, and the endpoints it describes should not be called. The repository is archived on GitHub.

things.title: POAP KINGS
things.summary: The website of POAP KINGS, Jamie’s family Clash Royale clan, publishing its roster, data, and season recognition.

observation.description: Proof of Arena Push — the official website for the POAP KINGS Clash Royale clan (#J2RGCRVG). Eleventy static site on GitHub Pages.

connections.label: runs
connections.detail: POAP KINGS runs Elixir Drop, its card-recognition and elixir-cost training game.

things.body:
POAP KINGS (#J2RGCRVG) is a Clash Royale clan that Jamie started in early 2026 with his son Tyler and Tyler’s cousin Levi. Jamie had [taken up the game](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/09/27/after-following-tyler-to-pokmon.html) in September 2025 as a newcomer, trying one of Tyler’s favorite games. In the [clan’s own words](https://poapkings.com/faq/), Raquaza and King Levy had cycled through clans that never quite fit, so the family built the clan it wanted: structure, recognition, and something lasting to show for the grind. Jamie claimed the [POAP KINGS Founder](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/02/05/poap-at-poap-kings-founder.html) POAP on February 5, 2026, and by July the clan had [reached 50 members](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/07/26/i-made-this-fun-slab.html) for the first time.

The name comes from POAP: the clan began by publishing POAP collectibles for seasons and milestones. When the POAP company and product stopped operating, the clan kept the name and the meaning it had taken on inside the clan, “Proof of Arena Push.”

Jamie asked Codex to [build the website](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/342/) from the notes the three founders had kept, and it was live quickly. It grew into an Eleventy site on GitHub Pages with a sortable roster, an interactive data page, member guidance, season recognition, and pages for the clan’s sister clans, Ship It! and Elixir Kings. The roster and war data come from Elixir’s JSON API, and the site promotes the tools the clan built: Elixir and Elixir Drop.

things.title: POAP2RSS
things.summary: RSS feeds of claims for any POAP drop or collector, retired when the POAP API went offline in July 2026.

observation.description: POAP2RSS creates a standard RSS feed for any POAP event. Drop an event ID in the URL and you have a live feed of new claims ready for any reader or automation platform. POAP2RSS makes POAPs more open, programmable, and connected to the wider web.

things.body:
POAP2RSS turned POAP activity into standard RSS: put a drop’s event ID or a collector’s address in the URL and get a feed of the latest claims, with the drop artwork and the collector’s ENS name or address as the author. Jamie issued many drops and wanted to know when they were claimed, and wanted to follow friends’ collecting in [Feedbin](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/07/04/seeing-poap-claims-show-up.html) and connect claims to automation services like IFTTT and Zapier. He had asked POAP for RSS in his [POAP Wishlist](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/01/14/poap-wishlist.html) in 2023 and again in [POAP + RSS = Awesome?](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/01/05/poap-rss-awesome.html) in January 2025.

In mid-2025 he built it himself, his first project with AI writing nearly all of the code. [Vibe Coding POAP2RSS](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/07/06/vibe-coding-poaprss.html) tells how: a throwaway prototype with Claude, a feature description researched with ChatGPT o3 and Deep Research, and then a Python AWS Lambda behind API Gateway. He declared it [officially launched](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/07/04/i-decided-to-declare-poaprss.html) on Independence Day 2025 and marked the occasion with a POAP. The [changelog](https://poap2rss.com/changelog/) records later changes: feeds grew from 20 to 50 items, inactivity notices waited 12 weeks and could be switched off, pagination arrived for large drops, and a green-screen redesign in February 2026. POAP2RSS fed the claim streams of the 612 POAP Challenge and the Airport POAP Rally sites.

The service read live claims through the POAP API, so it stopped working when POAP wound down. Jamie retired it in July 2026, archived the repository, and replaced the home page with a notice pointing to the POAP team’s archive at poaparchive.com, “with gratitude to Isabel, Patricio, and the whole POAP team.”

things.title: Proof of a Person
things.summary: Jamie’s POAP time capsule, 2021 to 2026, built from an archive captured after the protocol wound down.

observation.description: A time capsule and tribute to POAP through Jamie Thingelstad's collecting, issuing, and network
Jamie Thingelstad's POAP time capsule: collecting, issuing, writing, and network, captured after the 2026 protocol sunset

connections.label: tells the story of
connections.detail: The capsule’s writing traces POAP2RSS back to Jamie’s 2023 POAP Wishlist, where he asked POAP for RSS feeds. “RSS never came from POAP, so Jamie built it.”

connections.label: preserves
connections.detail: The 612 POAP Challenge drops are one of the series on the capsule’s Issued page, and the archive keeps a mirror of the challenge site.

things.body:
Proof of Attendance Protocol entered maintenance mode in March 2026 and wound down that summer. On 2026-10-17 Jamie captured his whole POAP life into a public [archive](https://github.com/jthingelstad/poap-archive): every token he collected, every drop he created, the people who minted them, and the posts and Weekly Thing sections he wrote about POAP from 2021 on. The tokens themselves stay on the Gnosis chain; the archive keeps the records and artwork that lived on POAP’s own services.

[Proof of a Person](https://poap.thingelstad.xyz/) is the time capsule built from that archive and published the same day. It counts 259 tokens collected, from the ENS 4th Anniversary vote on 2021-06-07 to an airport rally stop at Seattle-Tacoma in July 2026, and 130 drops issued, which 639 people minted. Each year from 2021 to 2026 is a chapter headed by a line from Jamie’s own posts. The pages show the timeline as two sides, what Jamie collected and what he made for other people, with a network of the people who hold his drops, his writing about POAP, and a short history of the company.

The site is a static Astro build from a JSON export of the archive. Drop artwork is served from a copy taken from POAP’s asset host while it was still up.

things.title: q2a-number-captcha
things.summary: A Question2Answer CAPTCHA plugin that asks for one digit of a nine-digit number written out in words.

observation.description: CAPTCHA Plugin for Question2Answer that requires finding a digit in a large number.

connections.label: protected
connections.detail: Jamie wrote the plugin to stop spam registrations on Ask Planet Kubb, the Question2Answer site he ran.

things.body:
Jamie had used [Question2Answer](https://www.question2answer.org/) for several years to run Ask Planet Kubb, and spam registrations were the problem. ReCaptcha let through four to ten spam sign-ups a day. The [Q2A Logical Captcha](https://github.com/amiyasahu/q2a-logical-captcha) plugin, to which Jamie had contributed a pull request, let through three to four times as many.

So he brought over the defense he was already using on his MediaWiki wikis ([Updated Dynamic Questy Captchas](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/10/28/updated-dynamic-questy.html)). The plugin spells out a random nine-digit number with the Numbers_Words PHP package and asks for the digit in one position, so the answer never appears in the page. It started as a modified copy of Q2A Logical Captcha. Jamie [released it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/16/questionanswer-number-captcha.html) on November 16, 2014 under the GPL v2, reporting that early results were great. The last change, in 2015, removed a PHP warning, and the repository is archived.

things.title: R/W Book Club
things.summary: A Minneapolis-Saint Paul book club meeting since 2003, and the website that keeps the record of everything it has read.

observation.description: Monorepo for the R/W Book Club: the public website, the shared knowledge corpus, and Oliver — the club's Discord agent.

connections.label: includes
connections.detail: Oliver is the book club’s agent and sixth member, sharing the same club database and corpus.

story.introduction: A long-running reading group, with a shared record.
engineering: The website presents the club’s reading history and members’ commentary.
Public llms.txt and llms-full.txt files make the reading record accessible to agents for analysis.
An iCal feed lets members subscribe to the meeting calendar.
Oliver, the club’s agent, generates the site from the club database and publishes it to GitHub Pages.
questions: How can an agent explore the club’s reading history?
How has the book club website evolved?

things.body:
The R/W Book Club is a group of technically minded readers who have met in the Minneapolis-Saint Paul area since April 2003. R/W stands for Read / Write: the members read, and many of them also blog. The club reads about eight books a year, mostly nonfiction, and members take turns picking the next book ([About](https://rwbookclub.com/about/)). Jamie built the website, not the club.

Jamie joined in late 2007, when his friend and former professor John Riedl, who started the club, emailed him about “this small book club of geeky guys” he was part of. Jamie “joined without hesitation” and shared the club with John, Tom, Erik and Dan until John died in 2013 ([Goodbye to my friend, John Riedl](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/07/21/goodbye-to-my.html)).

The club’s record has taken several forms. In early 2011 it was a MediaWiki site called the [Creative Computer Book Club](https://web.archive.org/web/20110323210256/http://creativecomputerbookclub.com/wiki/Main_Page); that July Jamie [hacked on MediaWiki](https://www.thingelstad.com/2011/07/15/i-had-a-blast-hacking.html) with the book club gang, and by January 2012 the same wiki was the [R/W Book Club](https://web.archive.org/web/20120106214958/http://rwbookclub.com/wiki/Main_Page) at rwbookclub.com. In 2017 he built a [Jekyll site](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/17/) at rwbook.club. The club has also kept its record in a shared Airtable database. The current site is generated by [Oliver](https://rwbookclub.com/oliver/), the club’s agent, and offers the reading record as llms.txt files for agents and the meetings as an iCal feed.

things.title: Reading Things
things.summary: A quarterly newsletter about books written by Jamie, Tammy, Mazie, and Tyler Thingelstad, sent four times from 2021 to 2022.

connections.label: was announced in
connections.detail: Jamie teased Reading Things in Weekly Thing 177 and announced it in Weekly Thing 186, a week after the first issue went out.

things.body:
Reading Things was a newsletter about books from the whole Thingelstad family. Jamie, Tammy, Mazie, and Tyler each wrote about what they were reading. Jamie teased it as “a fun, new family project” in [Weekly Thing 177](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/177/), and the [first issue](https://web.archive.org/web/20210508214912/https://reading.thingelstad.com/archive/reading-things-book-thief-atomic-habits-treasure/) went out on May 8, 2021. In [Weekly Thing 186](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/186/) he explained the plan: four emails a year, about books and things related to them, such as Tammy’s Corner and a bookstore challenge. There were no affiliate links, no tracking, and no “buy now” links.

Issues followed in summer and fall 2021. The [Winter 2022 issue](https://www.thingelstad.com/2022/02/06/the-winter-issue.html), sent on February 6, 2022, is the last one in the [archive](https://web.archive.org/web/20211130142318/https://reading.thingelstad.com/archive/) and the last one Jamie mentioned. In June 2022 he wrote about the [Reading Things First 100 POAP](https://www.thingelstad.com/2022/06/04/my-introduction-to.html) the family made to mark 100 subscribers. No public source says why the newsletter stopped, and reading.thingelstad.com no longer answers.

things.title: Release Notes
things.summary: A daily email with today’s version number; reply with notes from the day and they become that version’s release notes.

observation.description: Release Notes: a daily version-number email from Your Version Number; replies become the day's notes

things.body:
Release Notes is a daily email from Your Version Number. Each morning it gives the subscriber today’s number (“You’re 5.4.278 today”). Reply with anything about the day, or write it in the web app, and it is kept as the release notes for that version. Jamie [introduced it on 2026-10-08](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/08/in-i-wrote-about-your.html): after making the Your Version Number site he wished he got his version by email, and wondered what it would be like to add notes to each version.

It is lightweight journaling built around the reply. In [Weekly Thing 353](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/353/) Jamie wrote that he enjoyed getting the email each day and simply replying with notes, photos, and even audio. The [README](https://github.com/jthingelstad/yvn-release-notes) describes the rest: a writing streak and “On this day” notes from earlier releases in the email, tags and search, weather and places kept with each day, a Day One import, a full zip export, opt-in transcripts and photo descriptions, and owner-approved access for agents through MCP. The email tracks nothing and loads nothing remote.

It runs on AWS: a scheduled sender, SES for inbound replies, DynamoDB for notes, and a React web app with Hono functions on Lambda behind CloudFront. Its version arithmetic is a port of the Your Version Number site’s own code, checked against thousands of generated cases.

things.title: Road Sign Math
things.summary: A game of finding road signs whose numbers form an equation, begun as a blog in 2005, rebooted as a wiki in 2011 and as a blog again in 2023.

story.introduction: A little mathematics. A lot of looking around.
engineering: The original site, launched in 2005, had rules for play, a scoring system and scoreboards for players and states.
In 2011 it moved from a blog to a wiki so players could submit and maintain their own signs.
The 2023 reboot is a simple blog on Micro.blog that typesets each sign’s equation with MathJax.
questions: How did Road Sign Math start?
Why was Road Sign Math rebooted instead of relaunched?

things.body:
Road Sign Math is a driving game: find a road sign whose numbers make a valid equation, photograph it, and share it. It began with a sign on I-94 East toward the Twin Cities that Jamie passed coming home from visiting family in North Dakota, which listed distances of 3, 33 and 99 miles: 3 times 33 equals 99. On [Open Loop #1](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/1-big-fuzzy-dead-cat/) Jamie recalled that his friend Jim told him he should make a website, “and so that day I did a website.”

Jamie launched the site in February 2005 as a blog of signs, and other people sent in their own, so it gained rules, a scoring system and scoreboards for players and states. Signs came from all 50 states and most continents, including one from the Serengeti; by 2012 there were over 200. In 2011 he rebooted it for the first time, as a wiki, so players could maintain their own signs; an iOS app for capturing signs was considered but never built. In 2016, during a round of [technical downsizing](https://www.thingelstad.com/2016/05/03/technical-downsizing.html), he shut the site down and let roadsignmath.com expire ([Road Sign Math Rebooted](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/10/21/road-sign-math.html)).

In 2017 Jamie started a Jekyll site for the signs, [rsm.thingelstad.com](https://github.com/jthingelstad/rsm.thingelstad.com), on a stock theme. Jamie registered roadsignmath.xyz in 2021, and in October 2023 he [rebooted](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/10/21/road-sign-math.html) Road Sign Math a second time, back to a simple blog: “Just my signs. No scoring system or leaderboards.” New signs still appear, such as one in [September 2025](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/09/01/it-always-makes-me-smile.html).

things.title: Shortcuts
things.summary: Apple Shortcuts Jamie builds and shares, from the workflow that assembles the Weekly Thing to Micro.blog collection tools.

connections.label: assembles
connections.detail: A Build Issue shortcut runs a list of section shortcuts and combines the Markdown each returns into an issue, an approach Jamie has used since 2017.

connections.label: builds photo collections for
connections.detail: The Micro.blog Collection Creator, Copier and Viewer shortcuts use the Micro.blog API to populate the photo collections on Jamie’s blog.

connections.label: calculates
connections.detail: A shortcut Jamie wrote calculates his version number, and a daily automation shows it as a widget on his phone.

things.body:
Jamie uses Apple Shortcuts “everyday on nearly every device” to automate small tasks, write one-off scripts and build complex workflows, and he collects the posts about them on a [Shortcuts collection](https://www.thingelstad.com/collections/shortcuts/) page. Several are shared for others to install: [My QR Codes](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/05/21/my-qr-codes.html) (2023) puts a phone’s most-shared links on screen as QR codes, and [Launch Apps](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/09/30/launch-apps-shortcut.html) (2023) opens a Mac’s usual set of apps from the menu bar.

The largest is the Weekly Thing’s production workflow. In 2017 Jamie [assembled the newsletter](https://www.thingelstad.com/2017/06/23/assembling-the-weekly.html) with Workflow, the iOS app that became Shortcuts: a master workflow set the cutoff date, called one workflow per section, and stitched the HTML blocks they returned into an issue. In 2023 he [rebuilt it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2023/09/24/how-i-build.html) as native Shortcuts that return Markdown, with no Python steps, Data Jar to cache each section, and the S3 Files app to automate the photo section for the first time. In 2025 he added [LLM calls](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/03/09/how-i-use-ai-in.html) for jobs like suggesting subject lines and fortunes.

For his Micro.blog photo collections Jamie wrote three shortcuts in December 2024 and January 2025: [Collection Creator](https://www.thingelstad.com/2024/12/30/microblog-collection-creator-shortcut.html), which builds a collection from a clipboard of image links, Collection Copier, and Collection Viewer. He [shared all three](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/01/11/microblog-collections-shortcuts.html); they need a Micro.blog app token and the free Logger for Shortcuts app.

things.title: Thing Hugo
things.summary: A Micro.blog theme Jamie is building for his blog, with IndieWeb markup, Pagefind search, llms.txt, and links to Thingy.

connections.label: is being built for
connections.detail: Thing Hugo is a Micro.blog plug-in theme written for Jamie’s blog. The live blog still uses Tiny Theme by Matt Langford.

things.body:
Thing Hugo is a theme for [Jamie’s blog](https://www.thingelstad.com/), which runs on Micro.blog. It installs as a Micro.blog plug-in on top of the Blank design and is built for Micro.blog’s Hugo 0.158. According to its [README](https://github.com/jthingelstad/thing-hugo/tree/v2), it marks up every post and page with IndieWeb microformats, uses a single narrow serif column set in Newsreader and Source Sans 3, and builds in Tinylytics, Pagefind search, an `/llms.txt` file, a strip linking Jamie’s other sites, and an “Explore with Thingy” link under each post.

The repository’s `main` branch holds the first version, a Hugo theme for Micro.blog with Pagefind, llms.txt, and Weekly Thing and Another Thing signup boxes. The `v2` branch is a rewrite from October 2026. As of October 2026 the live blog still uses Tiny Theme by Matt Langford.

things.title: Thinglesbot
things.summary: Jamie’s Twitter robot, which posted home temperatures, solar panel status, and inbox counts from scripts around his house.
things.body:
Thinglesbot was Jamie’s robot, and it lived on Twitter. Jamie had scripts and tools like cacti watching things at home, but nobody looked at their output after a while, so he gave them a voice: a separate account, @thinglesBot, that posted the outdoor temperature four times a day along with readings from the attic and the utility room, said when the solar panels turned on and off, and reported how many emails were in Jamie’s inbox at the end of each day. It was “nothing more than a collection of scripts” on a few computers, posting with curl. Jamie [introduced it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2007/03/11/introducing-my-robot.html) on March 11, 2007, and two people he had never met, in other states, soon followed it.

When Jamie quit Twitter in November 2007 he wrote that [the robot’s account had been deleted](https://www.thingelstad.com/2007/11/04/buhbye-twitter.html), but Thinglesbot was [posting temperatures again](https://web.archive.org/web/20080218023438/http://twitter.com/thinglesbot/statuses/696031342) by February 2008. After it lost its sensor connections and went quiet, Jamie [rewired it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2009/03/24/my-robot-returns.html) on March 24, 2009, replacing the Bash and curl scripts with Ruby and the Twitter4R library and adding a daily favorite number, color, or letter and a “favorite follower.” Its posts were also collected on [thinglesbot.com](https://web.archive.org/web/20110209234653/http://thinglesbot.com/) (“I am Jamie’s robot”).

In February 2012 Jamie listed thinglesBot among the sites he [shut down](https://www.thingelstad.com/2012/02/08/shutting-down-some.html), and in 2014 among his deleted Twitter accounts ([Twitter Spam #NFL](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/28/twitter-spam-nfl.html)).

things.title: Things 4 Good
things.summary: The Thingelstad family’s yearly sale of hand-poured wooden-wick candles, with every dollar going to four nonprofits they pick.

observation.description: Things 4 Good — a handmade candle fundraiser site. Built with Eleventy.

story.introduction: Build something small. Do some good.

things.body:
It began with a wooden-wick candle. Jamie bought one at a market, loved its crackle, and by early 2020 had a box of supplies from The Wooden Wick Co. and was [making his own](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/137/). By the end of that year he had a [Wicky Thing Candles](https://web.archive.org/web/20201230115619/https://www.thingelstad.com/candles/) page with named scents like Lit, Cake Eater, and Man in the Pants. In September 2021 each family at Olson Family Vacation won a custom Wicky Thing candle in Tammy’s scavenger hunt ([WT194](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/194/)).

That fall the family turned the candles into a fundraiser. The first Things 4 Good Fall Fundraiser, on 2021-11-06 and 07, sold 134 Wicky Thing Candles in four scents, along with the first Jiggy Thing Puzzle, Four Bees Honey from Tammy’s sister Angie, and cookies Tammy and the kids baked. It [raised $4,757](https://www.thingelstad.com/2021/11/09/things-good-fall.html) for four nonprofits, one picked by each of Jamie, Tammy, Mazie, and Tyler, with buyers choosing how to split their donation. The name plays on the family name: four Things, four causes.

It became a tradition. In 2022 the family made 180 candles and [sold 172](https://www.thingelstad.com/2022/11/27/101105.html), raising $5,217. Totals grew each year, to $5,755 in 2023 and $7,010 in 2024, when the first day of the sale moved to the Mount Olivet Holiday Boutique. The 2025 sale, marked with a “5th Anniversary” POAP, sold 321 candles and [raised $9,048](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/11/16/things-good-candle-fundraiser-results.html), for [$31,787 over five years](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/11/16/things-good-five-year-impact.html). Each year Jamie posts the results and a look at the sale’s data. The candles now go by the Things 4 Good name, and every candle is still a $25 donation.

In 2026 the fundraiser got its own site, [things4good.xyz](https://things4good.xyz/), with the sale, every organization supported, and the numbers by year, all calculated from one dataset of sale events. The 2026 sale, the sixth, is set for November 7 and 8, with a new Maker Night where six guests pour their own candles.

Thingy is an AI librarian for Jamie’s public archive. You ask it a question, such as when he first wrote about Ethereum or what he was reading in 2019, and it finds the posts and issues that answer it, quotes them, and links to the originals. It knows only what Jamie has published. Weekly Thing subscribers sign in with their email, and Supporting Members get larger daily budgets.

Jamie previewed it in [Weekly Thing 346](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/346/) and launched it with the [new Weekly Thing website](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/07/massive-weekly-thing-website-build.html) on May 7, 2026.
