In September Jamie added photos and shared conversations and [called it complete](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/03/im-ready-to-call-thingy.html). In October it got [a new design](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/07/thingy-my-digital-librarian-got.html), with Claude Sonnet for subscribers and Claude Opus for Supporting Members.

Thingy answers from Librarian, which also offers the same tools to other AI clients over MCP. Since [Weekly Thing 350](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/350/), Thingy also writes two sections of each issue: Supporting Membership and Echoes, which connects the week’s topics to earlier issues.

things.title: VeloTweets
things.summary: A 2009 site that gathered professional cyclists’ tweets into one grid, built by Jamie, Luke Francl, Norm Orstad, and Chris Hatch.
things.body:
VeloTweets, “the Pulse of the Peloton,” collected the Twitter posts of professional road cyclists in one place. In early 2009 Jamie had started following riders such as Lance Armstrong through their RSS feeds and noticed that, read together, they gave a first-person view of the peloton during races. VeloTweets included only pro riders and a few others in the sport, added each rider’s team and nationality, and showed each rider once in a grid with their most recent message, so frequent posters did not crowd out everyone else. It also gathered TwitPic photos as VeloPics, kept a race calendar, and ran a Message of the Day tied to the day’s racing.

It was a side project with no budget and no business behind it. The idea was Jamie’s. Luke Francl did most of the development, in Rails 2.3; Norm Orstad designed the site; Chris Hatch built the list of riders and filled in their profiles; and Jamie “played sweeper,” helping wherever he could. The grid came out of a working session: Jamie credits Norm’s comparison to a baseball card, and Luke credits Jamie with showing one tweet per rider. Luke [announced the site on Rail Spikes](https://web.archive.org/web/20090514074605/http://railspikes.com/2009/5/10/announcing-velotweets) on May 10, 2009, and Jamie followed two days later with [Introducing VeloTweets](https://www.thingelstad.com/2009/05/12/introducing-velotweets-the.html) and [Why do Cyclists Tweet?](https://www.thingelstad.com/2009/05/12/why-do-cyclists-tweet.html).

The last Internet Archive capture of the working site is from [March 2010](https://web.archive.org/web/20100318125905/http://www.velotweets.com/); by [February 2011](https://web.archive.org/web/20110202042105/http://www.velotweets.com/) velotweets.com was a parked domain. In 2014 Jamie listed @VeloTweets among the Twitter accounts he had deleted ([Twitter Spam #NFL](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/28/twitter-spam-nfl.html)).

things.body:
The Weekly Thing is Jamie’s newsletter of links he found interesting, each with his commentary, plus his own blog posts from the week. He sent the [first issue](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/1/) on May 13, 2017, and has sent it most weekends since, taking breaks in summer and over the winter holidays. It began on TinyLetter, moved to MailChimp with [issue 23](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/23/) in October 2017, and moved to Buttondown with [issue 131](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/131/) in January 2020.

In May 2026, at 345 issues, Jamie [rebuilt the website](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/07/massive-weekly-thing-website-build.html) as a full archive with search, a table of contents for each issue, and Thingy for asking questions of the archive. Each issue also got an audio edition, published as a [podcast](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/podcast/). He built it with Claude Code, Claude Design, and Codex. Starting with [issue 350](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/20/i-just-published-weekly-thing.html) in September 2026, every issue has been written and sent from WT Builder.

Since November 2024, readers can become [Supporting Members](https://www.thingelstad.com/2024/11/17/weekly-thing-supporting.html). All of that money goes to one digital non-profit each year: Creative Commons first, then the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which [received $1,164.92](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/347/) in May 2026, and now [Signal](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/350/).

things.body:
WikiApiary is “a wiki to track other wikis.” Once a MediaWiki site is registered, a set of bots collects its software versions, extensions, skins, and editing statistics, and the wiki keeps the history so it can be charted and queried. It is built with MediaWiki and Semantic MediaWiki. Jamie started it as a holiday-break project in 2012; [MediaWiki.org](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/WikiApiary) dates it to December 21, 2012.

After its first year it was collecting from 9,555 active wikis and had stored more than 1.8 billion statistics samples, with over 3.3 million property values of its own ([One Year for WikiApiary](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/12/22/one-year-for.html)). Jamie called it the first project he started that grew a real community around it. Karsten Hoffmeyer helped administer it, Mark Hershberger explored ways for wikis to register themselves, Paul DeCoursey rewrote the chart code, and Federico Leva linked MediaWiki.org’s extension pages to their WikiApiary pages, which brought much of its traffic.

When Jamie decided he was done with it, others took it on. Mark Hershberger wrote in April 2017 that he had “[inherited the site from Jamie Thingelstad](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/HRNMPDZBNH5DWCWEFWMKLJAACDQDOAPY/).” That October, Hershberger and his son Basil began [moving it from the old Linode servers to Wikimedia Cloud Services](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/R7TRLEB73RKAGGA22VE3JAVW3YZOQSMF/). At its size the wiki has struggled with database timeouts: it [came back online](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/7HK7OPHOID3ZLCYSZTNPXDPG7MHTXGMV/) in March 2023 after an upgrade to MediaWiki 1.39, was [in write-only mode](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/AMVVOP72ONA2YI7XJ7KV6O3K42BBBES4/) by that September, and MediaWiki.org marked it not operational in February 2025.

In March 2026 Brian Wolff [got the site serving pages again](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/W5UMMJTSPGP7ZFT2NPTLCFHVVUXOLIOO/), with the update bots still off, and in May 2026 Hershberger announced from the Wikimedia Hackathon that WikiApiary and its bots [were moving to a Kubernetes cluster](https://lists.wikimedia.org/hyperkitty/list/wikiapiary@lists.wikimedia.org/message/DCSXARUPRRYZO4XKTTJXYIDM3T5AAGIV/) so it could start crawling wikis again.

things.summary: A Semantic MediaWiki site of nutrition facts for more than 20,000 foods, with a Twitter bot and an offline app.

things.body:
Wikinosh was a wiki of nutrition facts. Each food had a page with a nutrition label (serving size, calories, fat, sodium, carbohydrates, and protein) stored as Semantic MediaWiki properties, and foods were grouped into categories such as Baby Foods, Beverages, and Spices and Herbs. The Internet Archive first captured it in [December 2011](https://web.archive.org/web/20111205190345/http://wikinosh.com/wiki/Main_Page) with 13,753 food records; by [mid-2012](https://web.archive.org/web/20120630194132/http://wikinosh.com/wiki/Main_Page) it listed 21,550. In January 2013 [WikiApiary](https://web.archive.org/web/20130103025340/http://wikiapiary.com/wiki/Wikinosh) counted 20,433 articles and 981,167 property values on it.

In [Open Loop #2](https://www.thingelstad.com/projects/open-loop/2-what-am-i-editing-anyway/) in June 2012, Jamie described the food wiki he had “kind of in alpha” and how turning on Wikimedia Commons let a page show a photo of a banana just by naming the file. In July 2013 he worked with Yaron Koren to put Wikinosh’s data into Koren’s Miga app for offline, mobile access, and wrote up the Semantic MediaWiki limits he hit exporting more than 20,000 items ([Paging Large Datasets in Semantic MediaWiki](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/07/30/paging-large-datasets.html)).

The @Wikinosh Twitter account posted a random food from its 28,000-plus entries every six hours; in November 2013 one of those posts, about trout, drew an IRC-style trout slap from another bot ([Slapped with a Large Trout](https://www.thingelstad.com/2013/11/04/slapped-with-a.html)). The last Internet Archive capture of the wiki is from April 2014, and by November 2014 Jamie listed @Wikinosh among the Twitter accounts he had deleted ([Twitter Spam #NFL](https://www.thingelstad.com/2014/11/28/twitter-spam-nfl.html)).

things.body:
WT Builder is the authoring app for the Weekly Thing. Jamie started building it with Claude in July 2026 to replace the Shortcuts workflow he had used for nine years. It combines what he writes for an issue with links and posts pulled from Pinboard and Micro.blog. The issue stays structured until it is sent, and then WT Builder renders three different editions: the website, the Buttondown email, and the audio edition for the podcast. The [README](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wt-builder) says it is narrow on purpose: “one editor, one current issue, one newsletter.”

[Weekly Thing 350](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/20/i-just-published-weekly-thing.html), sent on September 20, 2026, was the first issue made in it. Jamie had Claude watch him use it that first time and fix problems as they came up. The next day they [reworked the audio edition](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/09/21/weekly-thing-podcast-improvements.html), with better pauses, section announcements, and pronunciation, plus links in the episode descriptions. In October Jamie [added an MCP server](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/10/03/my-newest-mcp-experiment-was.html) so Claude could follow along as he wrote and point out typos and grammar.

On October 11, 2026, WT Builder also [took over the Another Thing podcast](https://github.com/jthingelstad/wt-builder/commit/bea76c7ef4fc79a878072feebf694ce18ad217ea) from the retired Another Thing Builder. The Shortcuts workflow is kept as a fallback.

things.body:
For a few years Jamie had wondered about a book version of the Weekly Thing, something like an almanac. He [started it over Christmas 2025](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/19/i-just-finished-up-this.html) and [published it](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/20/i-made-a-book-yearly.html) on January 20, 2026, as _Yearly Thing 2025: Agents, Attention, Artifacts_. It gathers all 324 links he commented on across 31 issues in 2025 into ten topic chapters, from The AI Revolution to Tools, Productivity and Delights, with an Introduction, a Weekly Thing Index, and an Afterword. The eBook keeps every hyperlink. The paperback lists the issue each item came from, with QR codes that lead to the Weekly Thing Index.

He laid out the book in Vellum. The [paperback is $30 on Lulu](https://www.lulu.com/shop/jamie-thingelstad/yearly-thing-2025/paperback/product-84w66ey.html), and the first print copies [arrived on January 27](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/01/27/the-print-copies-of-the.html). The [eBook is $20 on Gumroad](https://jthingelstad.gumroad.com/l/yearly-thing-2025). Anyone who bought it in the first two months got a [Yearly Thing 2025 POAP](https://poap.gallery/drops/223594). All proceeds go to the Weekly Thing Supporting Membership program, and the book’s sales were part of the [$1,164.92 given to the Electronic Frontier Foundation](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/347/) in May 2026.

How is Release Notes related?

things.body:
In February 2018 Jamie wrote [Your Version Number](https://www.thingelstad.com/2018/02/24/your-version-number.html), building on a habit of his friend David Hussman, who gave his age as a version number. Jamie mapped it to semantic versioning: decades are the major version, years into the decade the minor, and days since the last birthday the patch. He was v4.6.52 that day, and he made a Workflow script to show the versions of people in his address book. David died that August; the [site’s About page](https://yourversionnumber.com/about/) says the arithmetic is his.

After a year of seeing his version through a [shortcut on his phone](https://www.thingelstad.com/2025/02/25/jamie.html), Jamie made it a website with Claude Code in May 2026, first shared in [Weekly Thing 346](https://weekly.thingelstad.com/archive/346/) on 2026-05-03 and then in [a launch post](https://www.thingelstad.com/2026/05/06/your-version-number-the-website.html). Add one or more birthdays, pick one of the themes, and the page shows each version, counting up at midnight. Everything is held in the URL, so a view can be bookmarked, set as a home page, or sent to someone, with no account. Cards with a signed note work the same way.

The Work Edition applies the same idea to a job: completed years of tenure, the quarter of the current tenure year, and weekdays into that quarter, with a build number that counts every business day, and work themes such as a board update. In October 2026 the idea grew into [Release Notes](https://notes.yourversionnumber.com/), a daily email of the day’s version with a journal attached.
